name: Social credit
summary: Social Credit is the monetary-reform doctrine of C. H. Douglas, who held that prices always exceed the incomes paid out in production, so debt-financed bank credit must fill the gap. He proposed a national dividend and a compensated price, funded by debt-free public credit, to give every citizen purchasing power and freedom from economic compulsion, while resisting centralised state and financial power. Later parties in Alberta, Quebec, New Zealand and Britain combined it with Christian and populist politics.
scope: Douglas's own doctrine (Economic Democracy, 1920, and the later Social Credit writings as summarised by Wikipedia), plus the Alberta experience as context. It does not represent the antisemitic conspiracy writings of Douglas's later years or the Manning-era Christian-conservative party platform as the core, though they colour a few low-confidence answers.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Douglas wanted consumers to direct production through their spending, which is market-like, but held that the banking system distorts prices; adherents split between free-enterprise and anti-market readings.

public-ownership.rationale: Douglas warned that nationalisation alone creates 'a worse, because more powerful, tyranny' and rejected collective socialism; the aim was to fix finance, not shift ownership to the state.

property-fundamental.rationale: Douglas defended individual economic freedom but treated the cultural inheritance and communal capital as belonging to all, so strong property absolutism does not fit; adherents split.

cut-welfare.rationale: The national dividend is an unconditional payment to every citizen, which is incompatible with cutting income support as dependency-inducing; later right-wing parties differed.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy never featured in the doctrine, and the Christian-conservative parties and libertarian-leaning individualists point in opposite directions.

strong-leader.rationale: Douglas wanted elected representatives to execute the electors' will and keep experts in their place, not rule by personal leadership; Aberhart's strong-premier style was a departure.

state-harmful.rationale: Douglas distrusted the state and wanted it to serve individuals, but he did not call for its abolition and wanted a National Credit Office and common-law courts.

empower-police-military.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

reviewHistory.rationale: The doctrine is silent; Douglas's anti-centralism and the later parties' law-and-order conservatism pull in different directions.

decide-locally.rationale: Douglas argued centralisation suits carrying out decisions but not deciding what to do, and praised decentralising tendencies; he sought decentralised power against the 'pyramid of power'.

gradual-change.rationale: Douglas proposed radical monetary reform by constitutional means and respected the common-law tradition, mixing reform of finance with institutional conservatism.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The founding doctrine did not address immigration; strands vary from restrictionist to indifferent.

nation-first.rationale: Douglas opposed export drives and international finance but also warned against centralised national power; he did not frame foreign policy as national interest versus cooperation.

limit-growth.rationale: Douglas held that production is abundant and the problem is distribution; he rejected limiting output and thought machines should free people from labour.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Douglas welcomed automation as displacing labour and sought to let the cultural inheritance of technique deliver leisure and abundance, once distribution is fixed.

revolution-justified.rationale: Douglas sought reform by constitutional and electoral pressure and feared Bolshevik-type centralisation; parties like Alberta's contested elections.

experts-over-public.rationale: Douglas wanted technical experts left free to run technical matters while the public sets the ends, so he sides with experts on how but not on what.

central-planning.rationale: Douglas held centralisation unsuited to deciding what to do and rejected collective socialism and nationalisation as tyrannical.

basic-income.rationale: The national dividend is a regular unconditional credit to every citizen on top of earnings, justified by the shared cultural inheritance and displaced labour; this is the doctrine's signature proposal.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Douglas condemned export-driven economics but his sources do not endorse protectionism as such.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Douglas opposed centralised direction and wanted consumers, not planners, to guide production; he criticised bank-directed investment but did not entrust it to the state.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Social Credit keeps money as a ticket system and keeps wages alongside the dividend; it reforms credit, it does not abolish money.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Douglas wanted money creation taken from private banks and given to a public National Credit Office, not left to the market.

one-party-rule.rationale: Douglas wanted to abolish party politics in favour of a union of electors directing representatives, so single-party rule is flatly opposed.

democracy-best.rationale: Douglas called for 'economic democracy' and defined democracy as the will of the people, though he disliked party and majority rule as practised; he supports it in his own sense.

direct-votes.rationale: Douglas wanted electors to fix the results they want while representatives carry them out, but not direct legislation on laws as such.

workers-councils.rationale: Douglas favoured consumer sovereignty and parliamentary pressure by electors; he saw shop stewards as decentralising but did not propose councils as a ruling body.

right-to-secede.rationale: Not covered; some Canadian strands, such as the Quebec créditistes and Alberta, held regionalist views, but there is no doctrine.

natural-rulers.rationale: Douglas stressed individual equality of access to the cultural inheritance and sought to make the people's will govern, but his respect for experts leaves a mild rather than firm no.

war-builds-character.rationale: Douglas argued that the financial system drives nations to war via export pressure and said full employment means war; war is an evil of the system.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Douglas's Christianity was philosophical, but Aberhart's Alberta was fundamentalist; adherents are split on legislating scripture.

military-superiority.rationale: Douglas saw war as a product of finance; later parties were not agreed on defence policy.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The core doctrine does not define the nation ethnically; antisemitic strands of the movement exist but they are not the mainstream position.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Douglas located the enemy in the financial system and the will to power rather than in class, and criticised collective socialism's misdiagnosis.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The dividend secures a baseline for all but Douglas held that incomes should still be earned; no equal outcomes aim.

civilizational-union.rationale: Douglas used Christian civilisation language but proposed no political union of civilisations.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Douglas stressed individual freedom but framed the economy as a service of consumers and called Social Credit practical Christianity, which does not praise self-interest as such.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Douglas insisted systems exist for people, not the reverse, and warned of an authority with no appeal; individual claims come first.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Douglas welcomed industrial productivity and held that only its financial accounting prevents it benefiting everyone.

restore-past-order.rationale: Douglas looked forward to an economy of abundance and leisure; Social Credit was a reform programme, not a restoration, though the cultural inheritance mattered to him.

direct-action.rationale: Social Credit worked by lobbying, leagues of electors and elections, not direct action against parliament.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Douglas valued machines and the cultural inheritance of technique as the source of abundance.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The dividend gives a share to all irrespective of work, but Douglas retained earned wages and price mechanisms; neither pure need nor pure work.

production-for-use.rationale: Douglas held the economy exists to deliver goods and services, not employment or profit, and criticised production for financial profit rather than consumption.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Douglas located the problem in the credit system and costs-versus-incomes gap, not in workers being exploited by owners.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Douglas condemned the exaltation of the state and the tyranny of centralised collective power.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Douglas argued that the price shortfall forces export drives that lead to war, though he blamed the financial system rather than capitalism as such.

taxation-theft.rationale: Douglas saw taxes as a poor substitute for issuing credit but did not call them theft.

harm-principle.rationale: Douglas prized individual freedom but did not set out a rule limiting state restriction to harm, so the doctrine is indifferent.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Douglas emphasised the right to leave unsatisfactory associations, but also made voting and the electors' will central.

positive-liberty.rationale: Douglas linked economic security with freedom and held that real freedom requires purchasing power and leisure, which the dividend supplies.

organic-representation.rationale: Douglas replaced parties with a union of electors and valued the constitution as a living organism, but did not propose corporate representation by family and trade bodies.

total-state.rationale: Douglas opposed the state as an authority with no appeal and warned of the Servile State.

national-rebirth.rationale: Social Credit promised a new economic era but not a national rebirth from decadence.

bound-labor.rationale: Douglas defended individual freedom and held that people's only inalienable property is their potential effort.

universal-morality.rationale: Douglas presented Social Credit as the policy of a philosophy and practical Christianity, implying universal moral truths.

single-common-good.rationale: Douglas appealed to the whole community's inheritance but stressed individual choice over any imposed single good.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Douglas held that bank debt makes up the price shortfall and that it should be met by issuing new national credit, not by austerity; deficits were less objectionable than debt to banks.

economic-freedom.rationale: Douglas stated that individual freedom, especially economic freedom, was the central aim, and linked economic security with freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Douglas wanted electors to dictate results and representatives to execute them, but wrote no theory of rulers leading by moral example.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Douglas described his policy as practical Christianity, which does not make reason the only guide.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Douglas held that the economy exists for goods, not employment, welcomed unemployment from machines and paid the dividend unconditionally.

class-collaboration.rationale: Douglas rejected class war as a diagnosis and placed the enemy in financial structures and the will to power.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Douglas held that the cultural inheritance is society's primary source of wealth.

dominated-front.rationale: A bloc of dominated countries against the West is foreign to the doctrine, which blamed international finance rather than Western states.

workers-nation.rationale: Douglas rejected class framing and so neither side of the question applies well.

ban-interest.rationale: Douglas attacked bank credit creation and debt rather than interest as such; some strands, influenced by usury critiques, would say yes.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Douglas saw the financial system and 'will to power' as the enemy rather than a class-run state.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Alberta's Social Credit era was tied to oil revenue, but the doctrine does not address energy policy.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The sources I read do not address immigrant assimilation, and strands of the movement differ on it.

elite-replacement.rationale: Mainstream Social Credit did not teach the replacement thesis; antisemitic strands did allege international conspiracies on other matters.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Douglas treated politicians as agents of banking interests and he criticised parties; populist anti-establishment tone runs through the movement.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for past security-force abuses is not a Social Credit theme in the sources read.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Douglas wanted a National Credit Office and a state making public activity serve the public, beyond minimal tasks.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Douglas held each individual has an equal share in the cultural inheritance and an equal dividend; it is implicit rather than argued.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Douglas was opposed to socialism, so the question does not arise.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Douglas defined democracy as the will of the people and wanted representatives to carry out electors' will.

trade-surplus.rationale: Douglas explicitly criticised the export of the product of labour and the drive to export caused by short purchasing power.

separated-powers.rationale: Douglas favoured common law supremacy to protect individual rights against parliament and viewed the constitution as a check on power.

vanguard-party.rationale: Douglas rejected centralised party leadership and wished to replace parties with electors, and criticised collectivism.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The dividend benefits all equally rather than prioritising the poor.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Manning-era parties were anti-union but Douglas's own position is undocumented in my sources.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Douglas held poverty in the midst of abundance results from the price shortfall and bank accounting, not population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The sources give no Social Credit view on ethnic diversity and cohesion; strands differ.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Douglas defended common-law protections of individuals against the state.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Douglas wanted a compensated price set by production efficiency, a rebate rather than a maximum price, and the movement's promises on price controls were mixed; adherents split.

party-controls-media.rationale: Douglas wanted the party system dismantled and individual freedom protected.

party-commands-army.rationale: Douglas opposed party politics and rule by parties.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Douglas wanted representatives bound to electors rather than to a party line.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Douglas feared centralised international finance and later alleged a conspiracy for world domination; supranational unions would worry adherents.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Reunification of divided nations is outside the doctrine's concerns.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Douglas treated the cultural inheritance of a society as its great asset but did not rank or equate cultures in the sources read.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Douglas valued individual choice but wrote no case against social conformity, so the doctrine is indifferent.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Douglas thought economic security and control of credit were needed for real freedom, but the statement concerns national independence and decolonisation, which he did not address.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Douglas made individual freedom the central aim and held scarcity to be artificial.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Douglas held that banks wrongly claim ownership of money they create and wanted money creation under the people's control.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial claims in peace deals are not a Social Credit concern.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Douglas criticised collectivism and nationalisation generally but did not analyse the Soviet system in the sources I read.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Douglas's practical Christianity and Alberta's Christian movement oppose it.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Douglas opposed any authority beyond appeal; though he saw British sovereignty in Trinitarian terms, a sacred head of state is not his position.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Douglas wanted credit issuance rather than tax changes as the remedy, and did not specify tax rate structures in the sources read.

character-from-environment.rationale: Douglas stressed the effects of the system on individuals but did not set out a theory of character formation.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Douglas argued for the supremacy of common law against parliament and the rule of law protecting individual rights.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Douglas called the constitution a living organism but the sources do not propose a mixed constitution in the classical sense.

leader-cult.rationale: Contrary to Douglas's anti-authoritarian view, but Aberhart's personal cult in Alberta shows a countertendency.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Douglas rejected the Marxist frame, so the question of class struggle under socialism does not arise in his doctrine.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Union of kin peoples across borders is foreign to the doctrine.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Douglas located the problem in the will-to-power and in policy rather than economic determinism, and appealed to philosophy and Christianity.

no-bailouts.rationale: Douglas attacked banking power, but whether to rescue failing firms is not covered.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Douglas favoured common-law supremacy to protect individuals against parliament, including majorities.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Douglas criticised export dependence, but did not propose closed blocs.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The movement was constitutional and electoral.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Douglas valued the constitution and monarchy yet also an inheritance common to all; no stated position.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Douglas credited accumulated cultural inheritance and cooperation rather than struggle as the source of wealth, and saw export rivalry as a path to war.

public-money-creation.rationale: Douglas held that bank loans create deposits and that banks wrongly claim ownership of the money they create; Social Credit reforms assign creation to a national credit office.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Douglas's cultural heritage is a common human inheritance rather than a national one, while later movements like Quebec's were nationalist, so adherents split.

patriotic-education.rationale: Douglas wrote little on schooling; Alberta's later Christian-conservative party may favour it but the doctrine does not.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Douglas argued the price shortfall grows and forces export drives and loan credit, so capitalism as financed is unstable; reform could save it.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Douglas distrusted party politics and wanted results set by the people, so parliament's supremacy is split.

office-by-exam.rationale: Douglas wanted experts to set technical methods while electors set results, but never backed examination for office; adherents are split.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The national dividend is a public, universal income funded by public credit, so pensions through private-company accounts cut against its core design.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Douglas wanted purchasing power raised so people can consume what industry produces, so he did not see consumption itself as harmful.

corporate-influence.rationale: Douglas attacked the concentration of financial and productive power and saw bankers' control of credit as the central abuse.

job-guarantee.rationale: Douglas held that machines make full employment unnecessary and the dividend should free people from compulsion to work, not guarantee jobs.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Douglas distrusted the centralised state, yet his hierarchical outlook did not deny a duty to obey; adherents would be split.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Douglas's later writings promoted antisemitic conspiracy claims but the movement's own parties disowned them, so adherents are split.

religious-nation.rationale: Douglas's Christian framing did not make faith the definition of nation; the parties were not confessional.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

reviewHistory.rationale: Douglas opposed collectivism and wanted individuals secure in their own means; common ownership of the means of production runs against this.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Douglas rejected both the existing banking-driven capitalism and collectivism, proposing a distinct monetary alternative.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Douglas's aim was freedom from centralised state and financial power, so suppressing opposition and independent bodies runs against the doctrine.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Douglas treated the export drive as a symptom of the domestic credit shortfall rather than a goal, so ruling territories for the ruler's economic gain is not part of the doctrine.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Economic democracy, consumers directing production and decentralised decision-making are central to Douglas's argument against centralised control.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Douglas appealed to Christian ideals and natural law, but adherents split on whether authority derives from God or from citizens' consent.

reification.rationale: Douglas argued that the financial system rules people rather than serving them, which partly matches this idea, though he did not use the Marxist concept.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Douglas attacked the centralised financial power of banks and wanted purchasing power spread through the national dividend, seeing concentrated control of credit as a threat to freedom.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Douglas never addressed it, and later Christian-conservative parties are split between traditional and egalitarian church views.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Douglas held that wages and salaries are insufficient to buy goods and proposed a dividend for all citizens, separating income from employment, but also valued work and rewarding useful production.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Douglas's later writings had a conspiratorial moral cast and Alberta's party was Christian, but the core doctrine is technical monetary reform; strands differ.

culture-before-state.rationale: Douglas's programme was a monetary and institutional reform to be enacted by existing governments, not preceded by cultural renewal.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Douglas focused on money and prices, not on who holds political power.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Not a point Douglas addressed; his remedy was monetary and left ownership of services open.

municipal-property.rationale: Douglas opposed collectivism and wanted private enterprise kept, with credit supplied publicly.

family-wage.rationale: The national dividend and compensated price were meant to give every citizen enough purchasing power to live.

person-over-state.rationale: Douglas's stated aim was individual freedom from economic compulsion and he resisted collectivism.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Later Social Credit parties, notably in Alberta and Quebec, were openly Christian, though Douglas's own writing is economic.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Social Credit's core doctrine is not racial, and a typical adherent would not organise by race.

farm-price-support.rationale: Douglas's compensated price and debt-free public credit aim to give producers fair prices and escape bank debt, and Alberta's Social Credit government backed farmers against creditors.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Douglas held that electors should demand results and leave methods to experts, and distrusted party politics, so procedure alone does not make a government democratic.

negative-income-tax.rationale: The national dividend is a universal cash payment given to every citizen as a right, which is close in spirit, though it does not shrink with earnings.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Douglas was not a scriptural literalist, though Aberhart's Alberta party was fundamentalist Christian; adherents are split.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Douglas opposed state socialism and centralised planning, wanting individual choice and financial reform instead of nationalised production.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Social Credit's national dividend is paid to every citizen universally rather than targeted at the poorest.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Douglas distrusted party politics and favoured policy set by consumers' demands, but Social Credit parties were party-based.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Adherents split: Alberta Social Credit was Christian-conservative while Douglas's own doctrine is not denominational.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Douglas did not address racial disadvantage and later adherents are split; no position can be sourced.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Douglas argued that machines displace labour and that the national dividend should let people work less while keeping purchasing power.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Douglas opposed centralised state planning and party rule, and wanted decentralised credit and individual freedom.

police-more-powers.rationale: The doctrine is silent; Douglas's anti-centralism and the later parties' law-and-order conservatism pull in different directions. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The national dividend is an unconditional payment to every citizen, which is incompatible with cutting income support as dependency-inducing; later right-wing parties differed. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Banks should not be allowed to create money by lending; new money should be issued by a public body.
missingStatements.rationale: Douglas held that bank loans create deposits and that banks wrongly claim ownership of the money they create; Social Credit reforms assign creation to a national credit office.

missingStatements.text: The prices of goods should be reduced by a public rebate so that consumers' incomes can buy all that is produced.
missingStatements.rationale: The compensated price, a rebate tied to the ratio of consumption to production, is a core Social Credit remedy for the gap between prices and incomes.
missingStatements.declined: A specific remedy (compensated price) of Social Credit doctrine; too narrow for a bank every audit must answer.

notes: Many answers are low-confidence inferences because the doctrine is about money and individual freedom. The William Aberhart link was not opened and the Aberhart key figure is sourced to the Social credit page. Strands differ sharply on social issues and on antisemitism.
